metaDescription: Convert a 5-field cron expression from one time zone to another, adjusting hours and days when it crosses midnight. Free, runs in the browser.
intro: Enter a five-field cron expression written for one time zone and get the equivalent for another, with the hour and, when the shift crosses midnight, the day fields adjusted.
why:
Many schedulers only understand UTC. A job that must run at 09:00 in Brussels then needs a different expression in summer and winter, and a late-evening job in New York lands on the next day in UTC, so the day-of-week field has to move too. Doing this by hand is where weekday jobs end up running on a Saturday.

This converter calculates the offset between the two zones on a reference date, shifts the hours and rolls the day fields forward or back as needed. It also warns about the daylight saving catch. A shifted expression is only right while both zones keep that offset. The work happens in your browser and your schedule is not uploaded.
howTo: Paste the cron expression with five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.
Enter the time zone it is written for and the time zone you want, as IANA names.
Optionally set a reference date so the correct daylight saving offset is used.
Copy the converted expression and read the notes about day shifts and clock changes.

faq.q: Will the converted job still be right after daylight saving changes?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The result is exact only while both zones keep the offset of your reference date. For year-round local time, set the time zone in the scheduler itself if it supports one.

faq.q: What cron syntax does it support?
faq.a: Standard five-field cron with lists, ranges, steps and day names. Complex expressions, such as a step on a half-hour offset, may need manual conversion, and the tool will say so.

faq.q: Why did my day-of-week field change?
faq.a: If the shift moves the time past midnight, the job runs on a different calendar day in the target zone. The tool moves each listed day forward or back by one so the job still fires on the intended day.
